sections.html:
Where Interstate 15 meets US-6 in Utah County, roughly 50 miles below Salt Lake City and 10 below Provo, Spanish Fork has the Wasatch Range on its east side and Utah Lake to the northwest. The city spreads over about 16 square miles at an elevation near 4,666 feet. Springville is about 4 miles northeast, Salem about 4.5 miles south and Payson about 6 miles southwest.

Population reached 42,602 in the 2020 Census, compared with 34,691 in 2010. Owners occupy about 80.4% of homes. Median value for 2020 to 2024 is $481,500, and median gross rent is $1,489. Think of the value as a survey midpoint; condition and lot can push your house in either direction.

New building adds competition. Permits in 2022 covered 810 new homes, 190 of them single-family and 620 multi-family, so anyone selling an older house is shopping against fresh supply.

Every Spanish Fork address is billed by Utah County, so the assessor, treasurer and recorder you deal with are all in Provo. Public schools belong to Nebo School District.

I-15 runs north to Salt Lake City and south toward Las Vegas, and US-6 heads east toward Denver through Spanish Fork Canyon. SR-51 and Main Street are the other gateways, and a Union Pacific rail line crosses the area. Mean commute time is 20.0 minutes by Census estimate.

Nebo School District has 15 schools inside the city: 9 elementary schools, 1 middle school, 1 junior high and 4 high schools. Spanish Fork High and Maple Mountain High are the main high schools, Spanish Fork Junior High and Diamond Fork Middle serve the middle grades, Landmark High is an alternative school, and American Leadership Academy is a K to 12 charter.

Winters average 66 inches of snow, which is why buyers scrutinize the roof and furnace. Know when each was installed.

Spanish Fork runs two separate water systems: drinking water for indoor use, and a pressurized irrigation system for lawns and landscaping. With a yard on the lot, expect the questions: does the irrigation connection work, and what does the summer bill run? The city also operates Spanish Fork Power & Light, with an average monthly residential bill of $77.11, and Spanish Fork Community Network for fiber, phone and cable. Natural gas comes from Dominion Energy.

The city permits a single ADU on each single-family property, provided the owner lives there. Because registration renews every year, anyone buying will ask for proof that the unit you are advertising is current.

ADU requirementRule
Lot sizeAt least 6,000 square feet
Barred zonesA-E, R-4, R-5 and R-O
Off-street parkingThree spaces for an internal ADU, four for a detached ADU
RegistrationEvery year with Community Development through CitizenServe, $60 fee
Impact fees and separate electric meterNot required

The Building Division can be reached at 801-804-4540.

sections.h2: Property taxes and who to call
sections.html:
Tax is billed by Utah County and due by the state deadline of November 30. Look for the bill in the mail from the middle to the end of October. An earlier valuation notice, sent before then, explains how to appeal to the Board of Equalization.

Whichever comes later, September 15 or 45 days after that notice is mailed, is your appeal deadline. A home you live in gets a 45% exemption, which leaves 55% of market value taxable.

Amounts still owed from earlier years do not appear on the current bill, so request a payoff figure from the Treasurer, who is at 100 East Center Street, Suite 1200, Provo, 801-851-8255. Payment is available online. The Recorder is down the hall in Suite 1300, 801-851-8179.

A buyer paying cash shows proof of funds in lieu of a bank approval, which leaves title work as the pacing item. A title or escrow company handles closing and sends the deed to the Utah County Recorder, and taxes are prorated to the closing date.

Heirs and job-movers often value a flexible closing date above a slightly higher price.

A seller who assumes the account is clean can be caught out, since earlier years' balances are missing from the present bill. Phone the Treasurer for a payoff number before you take any offer. Money owed is deducted from your proceeds at signing, and this year's tax is split between you and the buyer by days owned.

A valuation that looks too high can still be appealed within the deadline while the sale moves forward.

sections.h2: Selling a house with an ADU
sections.html: Paperwork decides whether an ADU helps or hurts. A registered unit with the owner on site, enough parking and a big enough lot (6,000 square feet minimum) is an asset. One that was never registered, or sits in a barred zone, is something you will have to disclose. Look up the registration with Community Development before listing, and renew it for $60 if it lapsed.

sections.h2: A cash sale, start to finish
sections.html:
First, describe the house: where it is, how old the roof and furnace are, whether irrigation runs, and whether an ADU exists. A written offer comes back. Set it against a listing's probable net and decide. Accept, and the title or escrow company starts its file and searches title while you settle on a closing day.

For the signing, gather photo ID, any mortgage payoff statement, the latest tax notice, ADU registration papers and every key and opener. With no lender involved, nobody keeps your date waiting for underwriting.

A listing makes sense when the house is in good shape and you can live with showings, an inspection and a buyer's lender. Cash makes sense when the roof or furnace is tired, the yard needs work, an ADU is out of compliance, or you simply need a date you can plan around. Ask for an offer, hold it up against what an agent expects you would net after commissions and repairs, and choose. Turning it down costs you nothing, and an offer carries no obligation.

New construction nearby gives buyers plenty of fresh options, so an older house with visible deferred work usually has to compete on price or on speed. A cash offer takes the repair estimates out of the picture, because the buyer already counts them in.

sections.h2: What Spanish Fork sellers usually run into
sections.html:
• An ADU with no registration, or one that breaks the lot rules.
  • Irrigation or yard faults a buyer spots on a walkthrough.
  • A roof or furnace worn down by years of heavy snow.
  • Money stretched thin because you have already bought elsewhere.
  • Back taxes nobody mentioned until the title search.

faqs.q: Is Spanish Fork in Utah County?
faqs.a: Yes. Utah County handles your property tax, valuation and deed recording, and Nebo School District runs the public schools.

faqs.q: When are Spanish Fork property taxes due?
faqs.a: November 30 is the last day to pay without a penalty under the state calendar. Utah County mails the tax notice between mid and late October.

faqs.q: How many people live in Spanish Fork?
faqs.a: The 2020 Census counted 42,602 people, up from 34,691 in 2010.

faqs.q: Can I rent out a basement apartment in Spanish Fork?
faqs.a: Only as a registered ADU. Spanish Fork requires owner occupancy, a lot of at least 6,000 square feet and annual registration for $60. Check the city's ADU page for the current rules.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Spanish Fork?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau reports $481,500 for owner-occupied homes in 2020 to 2024. That is a survey median, and your house may sit well above or below it.
